title: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions

learn.hook: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... Indian poets studied this pattern of rhythms centuries ago, long before it got the name Fibonacci. Can you guess what comes next?
points: A sequence is a list of numbers in a definite order. Each number is a term: a₁ is the first term, a₂ the second, and aₙ the nth term.
A rule for the nth term lets you jump straight to any term. For aₙ = 3n + 2, the 10th term is 3 × 10 + 2 = 32.
A recursive rule builds each term from earlier ones, like the Virahanka–Fibonacci numbers: each term is the sum of the two before it.
Famous sequences: square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, ...; triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, ...; cube numbers 1, 8, 27, 64, ...
Looking at the differences between terms often reveals the rule.

example.q: Find the next term of 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ... and a rule for the nth term.
steps: Differences: 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12

learn.reallife: Seat numbers in a stadium, the rows of dots in a rangoli and the beats in a tabla rhythm all follow sequences.

quiz.q: What is the next term of 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ...?
quiz.explain: The differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12: 30 + 12 = 42.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the last difference (10) the same, getting 40

quiz.explain: Each term is the sum of the two before it: 8 + 13 = 21.
quiz.mistake: Adds a fixed number or doubles instead of adding the last two terms

quiz.q: The nth term of a sequence is aₙ = 3n + 2. What is the 10th term?
quiz.mistake: Writes 3 next to 10 instead of multiplying, or adds instead of multiplying

quiz.q: If aₙ = n² − 1, what is a₅?
quiz.mistake: Computes 2 × 5 − 1 instead of 5² − 1

quiz.q: The triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ... What is the 7th triangular number?
quiz.explain: The nth triangular number is n(n + 1)/2. For n = 7: 7 × 8 ÷ 2 = 28. Or keep adding: 15 + 6 = 21, 21 + 7 = 28.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the 6th term (21)

quiz.q: A sequence starts with a₁ = 2, and each next term is twice the previous term plus 1. What is a₄?
quiz.mistake: Stops one step early and gives a₃ = 11

quiz.q: Which rule gives the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...?
quiz.mistake: Tests a rule on one term only instead of checking every term

quiz.q: Meena draws a rangoli with 1 dot in the first row, 3 in the second, 5 in the third and so on. How many dots are there in the first 6 rows altogether?
quiz.explain: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36. The sum of the first n odd numbers is always n².
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of dots in the 6th row (11) instead of the total

teach.ask: Gappu sees 3, 7, 11, 15, ...: "How can I know what the 50th number will be without writing them all?"
teach.praise: Find the pattern, write a rule using n, then put n = 50. No need to write fifty numbers!
teach.nudge: What is the same between one term and the next? Can you write that as a rule with n?

topics.title: Finite, infinite and partial sums; is it a term?

learn.hook: Is 100 in the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, ...? Don't list them all: let algebra check!
points: A finite sequence stops (the days of a week, 1 to 31); an infinite sequence goes on forever (all odd numbers), shown with '...'.
A partial sum Sₙ adds the first n terms: for 1, 3, 5, 7, ..., S₁ = 1, S₂ = 4, S₃ = 9.
To check if a number is a term, set the rule equal to it and solve for n. If n is a natural number, it is a term; otherwise it is not.
The solution n also tells you the position of the term.

example.q: Is 100 a term of tₙ = 4n − 1? Is 99?
steps: 4n − 1 = 100 gives n = 101/4 = 25.25: not a natural number, so no
example.answer: 100 is not a term; 99 is the 25th term

learn.reallife: A railway timetable lists a finite sequence of stations; the ticks of a clock form a sequence that goes on and on.

teach.praise: Brilliant! Solve 4n − 1 = 100; if n is a natural number it's a term, otherwise not!
teach.nudge: What equation do you make? What kind of number must n be?

topics.title: Recursive rules and the Virahanka numbers

learn.hook: How many ways can a drummer fill 5 beats with short (1-beat) and long (2-beat) strokes? Indian poets counted this more than 1200 years ago!
points: A recursive rule can use several previous terms. For example T₁ = T₂ = T₃ = 1 and Tₙ = Tₙ₋₁ + Tₙ₋₂ + Tₙ₋₃ gives 1, 1, 1, 3, 5, 9, 17, ...
Virahanka numbers: V₁ = 1, V₂ = 2 and Vₙ = Vₙ₋₁ + Vₙ₋₂, giving 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ...
Vₙ counts the rhythms of n beats made of short (1 beat) and long (2 beats) syllables: a rhythm of n beats ends in a short (leaving n − 1 beats) or a long (leaving n − 2 beats).

Virahanka (who lived some time between the 6th and 8th centuries CE) found them while studying Sanskrit poetic metres; Gopala (around 1135) and Hemachandra (around 1150) wrote about them before Fibonacci (1202). So they are often called Virahanka–Fibonacci numbers.

example.q: List all rhythms of 4 beats using S (1 beat) and L (2 beats).

learn.reallife: Tabla and mridangam players build rhythms from short and long strokes, the very patterns Virahanka counted.

games.title: Who and when?
pairs: Counted poetic rhythms, between the 6th and 8th centuries

quiz.q: What is the next Virahanka number after 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21?
quiz.mistake: Adds a fixed amount instead of the previous two terms

quiz.q: How many rhythms of 6 beats can be made from short (1 beat) and long (2 beats) syllables?
quiz.mistake: Stops one term early

quiz.q: Why is Vₙ = Vₙ₋₁ + Vₙ₋₂ for rhythms?
options: Because every rhythm has exactly two syllables
Each rhythm ends in a short (leaving n − 1 beats) or a long (leaving n − 2 beats)
quiz.explain: Splitting by the last syllable gives the two cases, which add up.
quiz.mistake: Cannot connect the rule to the counting

quiz.q: Tₙ = Tₙ₋₁ + Tₙ₋₂ + Tₙ₋₃ with T₁ = T₂ = T₃ = 1. What is T₆?
quiz.mistake: Adds only the last two terms

quiz.q: A sequence has u₁ = 2, u₂ = 5 and uₙ = uₙ₋₁ − uₙ₋₂. What is u₄?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order

quiz.q: Who among these wrote about these numbers before Fibonacci?
quiz.explain: Hemachandra (about 1150) came before Fibonacci (1202); Virahanka and Gopala too.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sequence was discovered in Europe first

quiz.explain: He counted the patterns of short and long syllables in verses.

quiz.mistake: Doubles the last term

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do you get the next Virahanka number?"
teach.praise: Yes! Add the two previous numbers!
teach.nudge: Which earlier terms do you use? What do you do with them?

learn.hook: Saving ₹10 more every week than the week before? Your savings make an arithmetic progression, growing by the same step every time!
points: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a sequence in which each term is got by adding a fixed number d, called the common difference, to the previous term.
d = any term − the term before it. It can be positive, negative or zero.
The nth term of an AP with first term a is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
To find which term equals a given number, solve a + (n − 1)d = that number for n.
The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d], or n/2 × (first term + last term).

example.q: Find the 15th term of the AP 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

learn.reallife: Auto fares that rise by a fixed amount per km, rows of seats that grow by 2 each row, and monthly EMI schedules are all APs.

items.text: The nth term of an AP is a + (n − 1) × ___
In the AP 2, 2, 2, 2, ... the common difference is ___
If a = 3 and d = 5, the second term is ___

quiz.q: What is the common difference of the AP 7, 11, 15, 19, ...?
quiz.explain: d = 11 − 7 = 4, and it stays 4 between every pair of terms.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the wrong way round, getting −4

quiz.q: Find the 20th term of the AP 3, 8, 13, ...
quiz.mistake: Uses n × d instead of (n − 1) × d, getting 103

quiz.q: Which of these lists is an AP?
quiz.explain: 5, 2, −1, −4 goes down by 3 each time, so d = −3 is constant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a decreasing sequence cannot be an AP

quiz.q: Which term of the AP 4, 9, 14, ... is 104?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add 1 at the end, answering 20th

quiz.q: Meena saves ₹50 in week 1 and ₹10 more each week than the week before. How much does she save in week 12?
quiz.mistake: Uses 12 × 10 instead of 11 × 10

quiz.explain: Pair the first and last terms: 1 + 100 = 101, 2 + 99 = 101, ... There are 50 such pairs, so the sum is 50 × 101 = 5050.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve, getting 10100

quiz.q: An AP has first term −6 and common difference 3. What is its 5th term?
quiz.mistake: Uses 5d instead of 4d, getting 9

quiz.q: A hall has 20 seats in the first row and 2 more seats in each next row. How many seats are there in the first 10 rows?
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of seats in the last row (38) instead of the total

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the 100th term of 2, 5, 8, 11, ... without counting forever?"
teach.praise: Start with a = 2 and add the common difference 3 exactly 99 times: 2 + 99 × 3 = 299. So quick!
teach.nudge: What do you keep adding? And how many times do you add it to reach the 100th term?

topics.title: More about APs: recursion, two terms, multiples and graphs

learn.hook: An AP plotted on graph paper lines up as straight as a cricket pitch!
points: Recursive form of an AP: t₁ = a and tₙ = tₙ₋₁ + d.
From two terms: if t₃ = 11 and t₈ = 26, then 5d = 15, so d = 3 and a = 11 − 2 × 3 = 5.
Counting multiples: the 3-digit multiples of 7 are 105, 112, ..., 994, an AP with d = 7, so n = (994 − 105)/7 + 1 = 128.
Plotting (n, tₙ) for an AP gives points on a straight line, because tₙ = a + (n − 1)d = dn + (a − d) is a linear polynomial in n with slope d.

example.q: An AP has t₄ = 18 and t₁₀ = 42. Find a, d and t₂₀.

learn.reallife: Taxi fares that rise by the same amount each km form an AP, and their graph is a straight line.

games.title: AP graphs
items: Points (n, tₙ) of an AP lie on a straight line.
tₙ is linear in n.
The slope of that line is the common difference.
tₙ = dn + (a − d).
Points of 2, 4, 8, 16 lie on a straight line.
That is a GP; the points curve upward.
The AP 10, 7, 4, 1 gives a falling line.
d = −3 is negative.
tₙ = 5n + 2 is an AP with d = 2.
d = 5; 2 is part of the constant.

quiz.explain: It is an AP with d = −3; only APs give straight lines.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If I know the 3rd and 8th terms of an AP, how do I find d?"
teach.praise: Spot on! Subtract the terms and divide by the gap in positions!
teach.nudge: How many steps of d are there between the 3rd and 8th terms?

learn.hook: Add 1 to 100 in ten seconds? Write the sum forwards and backwards, and every pair makes 101!
points: Write S = 1 + 2 + ... + n and also S = n + (n − 1) + ... + 1. Adding pairs, each pair is n + 1 and there are n pairs: 2S = n(n + 1). This idea appears in Aryabhata's work.
So Sₙ = n(n + 1)/2. Picture: two staircases of dots fit together into an n × (n + 1) rectangle.
The triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, ... are exactly n(n + 1)/2.
A block sum is a difference: 51 + 52 + ... + 100 = S₁₀₀ − S₅₀ = 5050 − 1275 = 3775.
To find the smallest n with Sₙ > target, test n(n + 1)/2 near √(2 × target). Some numbers are sums of consecutive numbers: 15 = 7 + 8 = 4 + 5 + 6 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5.

example.q: Find the smallest n for which 1 + 2 + ... + n exceeds 300.

learn.reallife: Stacks of pipes or cricket balls in a triangle pyramid at a shop have 1, 2, 3, ... per row: the total is a triangular number.

items.text: The dot picture of 2Sₙ is a rectangle of n by ___

quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2

quiz.mistake: Thinks the pairs sum to n

quiz.explain: n by n + 1 = 7 by 8, which holds 56 dots = 2 × 28.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the staircases make a square

quiz.mistake: Multiplies 30 by 30

teach.praise: Superb! Pair the numbers to make 101 fifty times: 5050!

learn.hook: A king once promised a wise man 1 grain of rice on the first chessboard square, 2 on the next, 4 on the next... By the last square it was more rice than the whole world had!
points: A geometric progression (GP) is a sequence in which each term is got by multiplying the previous term by a fixed non-zero number r, called the common ratio.
r = any term ÷ the term before it.
The nth term of a GP with first term a is aₙ = a × r^(n − 1).
If r > 1 the terms grow very fast (doubling, tripling). If 0 < r < 1 they shrink, like a bouncing ball.
An AP grows by adding the same amount; a GP grows by multiplying by the same amount.

example.q: Find the 6th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, 24, ...

learn.reallife: Bacteria doubling every hour, a viral video being shared, and money growing with compound interest all follow geometric progressions.

games.title: GP true or false
items: In a GP, you multiply by the same number each time
That fixed multiplier is the common ratio r.
It adds 2 each time, so it is an AP. 4 ÷ 2 = 2 but 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5.
The common ratio of 81, 27, 9, 3 is 1/3
27 ÷ 81 = 1/3, and every next ratio is also 1/3.
Starting from 1, the GP with r = 2 eventually overtakes the AP with d = 100
Doubling eventually beats adding a fixed amount. The 20th term of the GP is 2¹⁹ = 524288, while the AP's 20th term is only 1901.
The nth term of a GP is a × r × n
It is a × r^(n − 1), a power, not a product with n.

quiz.q: What is the common ratio of the GP 3, 12, 48, 192, ...?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts terms (12 − 3 = 9) as if it were an AP

quiz.q: What is the next term of 5, 10, 20, 40, ...?
quiz.mistake: Adds the last difference (20) instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Find the 6th term of the GP 2, 6, 18, ...
quiz.mistake: Uses r⁴ (getting 162) or r⁶ (getting 1458)

quiz.q: Which of these is a GP?
quiz.explain: Each term is the previous one divided by 3, that is, multiplied by r = 1/3.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a GP must be increasing

quiz.q: A lab starts with 50 bacteria, and the number doubles every hour. How many bacteria are there after 5 hours?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 50 by 5 instead of doubling five times

quiz.q: What is the common ratio of 64, 32, 16, 8, ...?
quiz.explain: r = 32 ÷ 64 = 1/2. The terms halve each time.
quiz.mistake: Divides the earlier term by the later one, getting 2

quiz.q: A ball dropped from 81 m bounces back to 2/3 of its previous height each time. How high does it rise after the 3rd bounce?
quiz.mistake: Stops at the 2nd bounce (36 m) or goes one too far (16 m)

quiz.q: Aisha sends a Diwali greeting to 3 friends. Each of them forwards it to 3 new people, and so on. How many new people receive it in round 5?
quiz.explain: Round 1: 3, round 2: 9, round 3: 27, round 4: 81, round 5: 243. That is 3⁵.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 3 × 5 instead of raising 3 to the power 5

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: "2, 4, 6, 8 and 2, 4, 8, 16 both start with 2, 4. Why is one an AP and the other a GP?"
teach.praise: In an AP you add the same number each time; in a GP you multiply by the same number each time. 2, 4, 6, 8 adds 2, but 2, 4, 8, 16 doubles!
teach.nudge: From 4 to the next term, did you add something or multiply by something?

learn.hook: Multiply by −2 each time and the sequence jumps back and forth across zero!
points: Recursive form of a GP: t₁ = a and tₙ = r × tₙ₋₁.
The ratio r can be greater than 1 (growth), between 0 and 1 (shrinking), negative (signs alternate) or even irrational, like √2: 1, √2, 2, 2√2, 4, ...
To test for a GP, check that each term ÷ the previous term gives the same r. To find which term equals k, solve a × rⁿ⁻¹ = k.
Three terms in a GP can be taken as a/r, a, ar. Their product is a³, which quickly gives a; then a sum condition gives r.

example.q: Three numbers in a GP have product 216 and sum 21. Find them.
steps: Take a/r, a, ar: product a³ = 216, so a = 6

learn.reallife: A savings scheme that doubles your money every 8 years makes a GP of amounts.

quiz.q: A GP has t₁ = 4 and tₙ = 3tₙ₋₁. What is t₄?
quiz.mistake: Adds 3 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: What is the common ratio of 2, −6, 18, −54, ...?
quiz.mistake: Ignores the alternating sign

quiz.q: In the GP 1, √2, 2, 2√2, ..., what is the 9th term?
quiz.mistake: Uses n instead of n − 1 as the power

quiz.q: Which term of the GP 3, 6, 12, ... is 384?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the n − 1
Checks only the first ratio

quiz.q: A GP has ratio 1/2 and first term 64. What is t₅?
quiz.mistake: Uses the 4th power for t₄

quiz.q: Three terms of a GP have product 64. What is the middle term?
quiz.mistake: Divides 64 by 3

quiz.q: Three terms a/r, a, ar of a GP have product 1000 and sum 35. What are they?
quiz.mistake: Picks numbers with the right sum but not a GP

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I check if a sequence is a GP?"
teach.praise: Great! Divide each term by the one before; if the ratio is always the same, it's a GP!
teach.nudge: What do you divide? What must be true about all the ratios?

learn.hook: Zoom into a cauliflower floret and you see a tiny cauliflower. That's a fractal!
points: Sierpinski triangle: start with a shaded triangle, join the midpoints and remove the middle one; repeat in each shaded triangle.
After n steps there are 3ⁿ shaded triangles, and the shaded area is (3/4)ⁿ of the original: both are GPs.
Sierpinski carpet: split a square into 9 and remove the centre; repeat. After n steps there are 8ⁿ squares and the area left is (8/9)ⁿ, which gets closer and closer to 0.
Fractals in nature: tree branches, ferns, cauliflower and romanesco, snowflakes, river networks and coastlines repeat similar shapes at smaller scales.

example.q: After 3 steps of the Sierpinski triangle, how many shaded triangles are there and what fraction of the area is shaded?

learn.reallife: Designers use fractal patterns in rangoli, textiles and even mobile phone antennas.

teach.praise: Wonderful! It repeats the same pattern at smaller and smaller sizes!
teach.nudge: What happens inside each small triangle? Does the pattern repeat?

topics.title: Graphs of GPs and the bouncing ball

learn.hook: Drop a ball from 16 m: it bounces to 8, then 4, then 2... Does it ever stop travelling?
points: Plotting (n, tₙ) for a GP gives points on a curve, not a straight line.
With r > 1 the curve shoots up faster and faster; with 0 < r < 1 it drops quickly and then flattens out towards 0.
Bouncing ball: if a ball dropped from height h bounces to r × the height each time, the bounce heights hr, hr², hr³, ... form a GP.

Total distance = first drop + 2 × (sum of bounce heights), because the ball goes up and comes down each bounce. For h = 16, r = 1/2: bounce heights 8 + 4 + 2 + ... approach 16, so the total approaches 16 + 32 = 48 m.

example.q: A ball is dropped from 16 m and bounces back to half its height each time. How far has it travelled when it hits the ground for the 3rd time?

learn.reallife: Sports scientists test cricket and tennis balls by measuring how high they bounce: a fixed bounce ratio gives a GP.

games.title: Graphs and bounces
items: The points of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 lie on a straight line.
They lie on a curve that bends upward.
A GP with r = 1/2 gets close to 0 but never reaches it.
Halving a positive number never gives 0.
A ball's bounce heights with a fixed ratio form an AP.
Multiplying by a fixed ratio gives a GP.
Total distance counts each bounce height twice.
Up and back down.
The graph of an AP is a curve.
An AP gives a straight line.

quiz.q: Which sequence's graph of (n, tₙ) is a curve that rises faster and faster?
quiz.explain: A GP with r > 1 grows faster each step.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an AP rises faster

options: drops quickly and flattens out towards 0
quiz.explain: A GP with 0 < r < 1 shrinks by a factor each time.
quiz.mistake: Expects the terms to become negative

quiz.q: A ball dropped from 20 m bounces to 3/5 of its height each time. How high does it rise after the 2nd bounce?
quiz.mistake: Uses only one bounce

quiz.q: A ball dropped from 10 m bounces to half its height each time. How far has it travelled when it lands the 2nd time?
quiz.mistake: Counts the bounce only once

quiz.q: For the same ball (10 m, half each time), the bounce heights 5 + 2.5 + 1.25 + ... approach which total?
quiz.explain: Each half fills half of what is left: the sum approaches 10.
quiz.mistake: Thinks infinitely many bounces mean infinite distance

quiz.q: So what total distance does that ball approach if it bounces forever?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the bounces

quiz.q: A ball dropped from 81 m rebounds to 1/3 of the height each time. After which bounce does it first rise less than 2 m?
quiz.explain: Heights: 27, 9, 3, 1. The 4th bounce is the first below 2 m.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 3 m

quiz.q: Why does the graph of a GP never look like a straight line (for r ≠ 1)?
options: The terms change by multiplying, so the gaps between them change
Because GPs have no first term
Because the points are too far apart
quiz.explain: In a line, equal steps in n give equal gaps; in a GP the gaps grow or shrink.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sequence makes a line

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the total distance a bouncing ball travels?"
teach.praise: Perfect! First drop, plus each bounce height twice!
teach.nudge: Does the ball travel each bounce height once or twice? Don't forget the first drop!
